chapter_theme: The battle of the Manmagal ilampakam at its height: Govindan, Ulokapalan, Nabulan, Vipulan and Padumukan kill or rout the allied kings, Nabulan and Vipulan refuse to strike the frightened, the weaponless, the wounded, the young and the old, and Vipulan's single duel ends with the slain challenger received into heaven.

cast.role: the king who leads Civakan's war (கோவிந்த னென்னுஞ் சிங்கம் 2252; hailed கோவிந்தன் வாழ்க in 2277)
a king on the enemy side, killed with his elephant by Govindan
the prince of Chandirapam in the Pallava country, Civakan's friend; named உலோக பாலன் in 2255 and பல்லவ தேச மன்னன் in 2253
the king of Kampili, fighting on the enemy side and killed by Ulokapalan
the king of Magadha, on the enemy side, whom Nabulan spares
an unarmed young warrior on the enemy side who claps and shouts a challenge at Nabulan
one of Civakan's companions, brother of Nabulan
the kings fighting on the enemy side, whom Vipulan challenges
the warrior who challenges Vipulan to single combat and is killed
the celestial women who receive warriors slain in battle
Civakan's friend, fighting from an elephant
a warrior on the enemy side, killed by Padumukan
a warrior on the enemy side who charges to avenge Kamukan
the fighting men of the armies
a boasting prince on the enemy side killed by Padumukan's arrow
a named war elephant whose tusks break in the charge

2252.reading: Govindan, a lion among chariot-bowmen, strikes with blazing gold-worked arrows until the king called Marattan, a mountain of gold, comes down and falls with his elephant in a cloud of gold dust.
2252.nuance: The fallen king is likened to a gold hill, so the dust of his fall is gold dust: the praise of the enemy's splendour measures the victor's arrows.
2252.event: Govindan's arrows bring down the Maratta king together with his elephant.

2253.reading: The elephant ridden by the king of the Pallava country, on whose trappings gold lies like kongu flowers shed on a hill, closes with the tusker ridden by the lord of Kampili.
2253.nuance: The Pallava king is named Ulokapalan only in 2255 (மற்றவ னுலோக பாலன்); the identification of the two is a reading of that line.
2253.event: The Pallava king's elephant and the Kampili king's elephant clash.

2254.reading: The tusks strike so hard that fire leaps from them and burns the priceless yak-tail whisks, and the heroic king beats back with his lance the rain of arrows that hides the sky and roars like Death.
2254.nuance: Which king wards off the arrows is not said; the next verse's மற்றவன் ('the other one') for Ulokapalan suggests this one is the Kampili king.
2254.event: The Kampili king wards off a rain of arrows with his lance.

2255.reading: The other, Ulokapalan, pulls out the arrow shot into his gold-banded forehead, and the blood that gushes onto the foe's elephant makes him look like the rising sun stretching out a single great ray.
2255.nuance: The wound is turned into ornament: the jet of blood becomes the sun's first ray, so the verse makes the hurt a sign of glory rather than of danger.
2255.event: Ulokapalan plucks an arrow from his own forehead and fights on.

2256.reading: The conqueror bends his bow until it bows, and his arrows sink into the chest that the breasts of soft-spoken women once ploughed, so that the Kampili king falls like a lion while his sea-like army scatters.
2256.nuance: The arrows enter exactly where the women's breasts lay: love's marks on the chest become the place of death, an image the chapter repeats (2273).
2256.event: Ulokapalan's arrows kill the king of Kampili, and his army breaks.

2257.reading: Nabulan, whose body glows like a hill of golden kongu blossom and whose beauty passes even Mal's, raises a lightning-bright spear and makes his maned horse leap onto the brow of the Magadha king's elephant.
2257.event: Nabulan rides his horse up onto the Magadha king's war elephant.

2258.reading: When the lord's eyes flicker in fear, the swordsman, ashamed, holds back his blow, laughs, tells him not to be afraid since he is not angry, and swiftly makes his horse spring like a tiger onto another elephant.
2258.nuance: The shame (நாணி) is the victor's, not the loser's: to strike a man who flinches would dishonour the striker. ஏந்தறன் (line 1) is read as ஏந்தல் தன், the lord's.
2258.event: Nabulan spares the frightened Magadha king, reassures him, and turns to another elephant.

2259.reading: When a youth with no weapon in his hand claps and shouts, the young man, ashamed because his foe's arms have fallen, will not strike even his elephant, and turns back like the desire of a man with no money who hovers round the beauty of dark-eyed women.
2259.nuance: The simile is unexpected and exact: the warrior who meets no fit foe is like a penniless lover who can only look at courtesans, a desire with nothing to spend itself on. The young man who claps is read as an enemy youth; that he is the same as Nabulan is unlikely since line 4 names the one who turns back காளை.
2259.event: Nabulan refuses to fight a weaponless youth who challenges him, and withdraws.

2260.reading: Vipulan asks the enemy: is there among you anyone who, finding no joy in guarding the earth, would rather guard heaven and leave his fame behind here; and his spear, flashing like lightning in dark night, raised high where the vultures wait, puts the question too.
2260.nuance: The taunt is courteous in form, an offer of heaven; line 4 (கண்காவல கழுகோம்புவது) is hard to construe, and the reading that the vultures guard the spear's point is a guess.
2260.event: Vipulan challenges the enemy kings to come and die.

claims.claim: a warrior who dies in battle leaves his fame on earth and takes up the guarding of heaven

2261.reading: The spear-ploughman does not strike even a rutting elephant, since a beast brings no distinction; nor a wounded man, even an equal, since he is another's leavings; nor the young, since without a match valour withers; nor the old, since they lack strength.
2261.nuance: Every reason is the striker's honour, not the victim's need: the wounded are refused as leftovers (மிச்சில்), the young because valour would wither, so the restraint is pride as much as mercy. The next verse (2262) at once qualifies the first rule: he will take on elephants if they fall many to one blow.

claims.claim: a warrior should not strike a beast, since there is no distinction in it
a man already wounded by another is not to be struck, being another's leavings
a warrior should not strike the young or the old, who are no match for him

2262.reading: Asking whether there are rutting elephants, one or many, worth felling in a single stroke, the angry spearman goes like a tiger cub of the golden slopes, bees humming in his garland, and a thousand hostile elephants flee.
2262.event: Vipulan seeks out elephants, and a thousand of them flee before him.

2263.reading: A man with long earrings, a gold ear-leaf, a waist-string and a shining sword comes up and says 'strike, you who have no equal'; the hero laughs 'is that so?' and, glowing with manly beauty, says 'here at last is my match'.
2263.nuance: The speakers of the two short speeches are not named; the challenger is read as the ஒருவன் of line 2 and the one who laughs as Vipulan.
2263.event: A warrior challenges Vipulan to single combat and Vipulan accepts him as a match.

2264.reading: Like two young suns at war on the waves of sweet water, whirling with lightning between them as if at play, the two, with gold bowstrings, matchless bows, shields and killing swords, garlands and banner-marked chests, circle each other.
2264.event: Vipulan and his challenger circle each other in the duel.

2265.reading: 'You are my guest; strike', says one, offering his fragrant chest, and the other strikes and breaks his dark ornament; 'now it is your turn', and the blazing spear cleaves the challenger through the middle so that he stands unaware of it; the celestial women shower flowers and bow, and he reaches heaven.
2265.nuance: ஊழ் in line 2 (நினதூழினி) means 'turn', not fate. The duel is framed as hospitality: the first blow is the guest's portion. Heaven goes to the man who loses, not the victor. Who says which line is a reading.
2265.event: Vipulan lets the challenger strike first, then kills him with one blow, and the dead man is received into heaven.

claims.claim: a warrior slain fighting fairly is welcomed by the celestial women and goes to heaven

2266.reading: Padumukan, his body glowing like a heap of pearls and his chest hung with rows of ornaments, mounted on a triple-rutting elephant with a gold forehead plate, raises his spear and blazes with anger on seeing Kamukan.
2266.event: Padumukan sights Kamukan and moves against him in anger.

2267.reading: After the enemy army attacked and tired, the hard-eyed fighting men, showing strength and manhood, gave up their lives and fell, lying everywhere like young sharks cast up when the wind beats the sea and it breaks.
2267.nuance: Which army's men fall is unclear; மாற்றவன் சேனை may be the subject of தாக்கி or its object.
2267.event: Warriors of both sides fall in numbers on the field.

2268.reading: As the army sways and runs like the swing of women at play, Padumukan drives his elephant and, as the full moon enters the brow of a cloud, drives a discus into the brow of the furious elephant.
2268.nuance: ஆழி is read as a discus or wheel-weapon; the brow it enters is read as Kamukan's elephant's.
2268.event: Padumukan drives a weapon into the forehead of Kamukan's elephant.

2269.reading: Unable to bear that great strength, Kamukan raises a javelin, and as it sinks into the temple of the rutting elephant like a peacock's tail on a mountain's brow, the lord, enraged, takes the young man with his sword.
2269.nuance: Read with 2270, the young man taken (காளையை வெளவினான்) is Kamukan, who falls in the next verse; the verse names neither.
2269.event: Kamukan wounds Padumukan's elephant with a javelin, and Padumukan kills him with his sword.

2270.reading: When Kamukan, lover of the anklet-wearing women whose spear-like eyes spit fire, falls on the field, Komukan, his armour flashing and garland on his chest, points with his fingertip and drives his killing elephant on like Death.
2270.nuance: The name Kamukan is played on: he is the காமுகன், the lover, of the women with anklets, so his fall is also their loss.
2270.event: Kamukan falls, and Komukan charges Padumukan to avenge him.

2271.reading: The elephants wheel and churn the field, the roaring flood of blood on the earth mixes with the dust, rises on a mighty wind and covers the sky, so the heavens are hung with blood like a painted battle scene.
2271.nuance: The simile reverses art and life: the real field is compared to a painting of a field, so the slaughter is seen as a spectacle.

2272.reading: His hand goes to the quiver, his eyes redden and brows arch, the bent bow sends the arrows straight and lives depart; then victorious arrows sink in and cover his body, and Komukan appears like coral on a lightning-touched hill.
2272.nuance: Whether lines 1 to 2 describe Komukan shooting or Padumukan shooting him is not clear; the coral image means he is red with blood, and the verse does not say he dies.
2272.event: Komukan shoots and kills, then is himself covered with arrows.

2273.reading: Like a beautiful coral branch growing on a snow mountain, the elephant whose curved tusks are dipped in blood is driven in to seize him, and the man whose chest is flushed from pressing women's bright breasts rages and scatters burning arrows.
2273.nuance: The two images of red (coral, the flushed chest) join love and slaughter in one figure; who is described is not named, and he is read as Padumukan.
2273.event: A warrior on an elephant presses the attack, shooting burning arrows.

2274.reading: Like fire spreading over a hill of cotton, with both his hands and with his great-trunked elephant he drinks the sweet lives of the army, routs and drives it, and the elephant-rider, his fierce strength showing, roars.
2274.event: Padumukan routs the enemy army and roars in triumph.

2275.reading: As a prince roars in pride, the lord bends his bow and with one arrow tears through his hand, his mouth and his heart so that the feathered end shows; and as the lord shoots, the elephant, its tusk breaking, gores and its strength is spent.
2275.nuance: உடு is read as the arrow's feathered butt and வயிரம் as the elephant's hardness or fury; both are doubtful, and the elephant's part in lines 3 to 4 is unclear.
2275.event: Padumukan kills a boasting prince with a single arrow, and the prince's elephant is broken.

2276.reading: When the long-rutting elephant called Nittilamanivandu charges, its pearl-bearing tusks break at once, as an elephant falls on a hill that flows with pearls and its fury ends there; the last line, with ear ornaments flashing, is broken.
2276.nuance: Line 4 is a foot short and its first words repeat the opening of 2277 (பத்திரக் கடிப்பு மின்ன), so the end of the verse may be lost.
2276.event: The elephant Nittilamanivandu charges and breaks its tusks.

links.note: The Kural's hero pulls the spear from his own body and laughs; Ulokapalan plucks the arrow from his forehead and the gushing blood is likened to the dawn sun's first ray.
links.teaches: Together they show the wound pulled from the body as a fixed sign of the hero, and that the epic turns the Kural's psychological shock, a laugh, into visual glory, so the same act is valued as composure in the one and as splendour in the other.

gains.a: the forehead-arrow is recognised as a stock heroic act, not a chance detail, which explains why the verse lingers on it before the kill
gains.b: the couplet's bare gesture gains a full scene with its consequence: the man who pulls the arrow is the one who kills in the next verse

links.note: The Kural says help to a foe in misfortune is the cutting edge of valour; Nabulan, seeing the Magadha king flinch, holds his blow, reassures him and goes elsewhere.
links.teaches: The couplet calls kindness to a stricken foe valour's sharpest point, and the epic shows what drives it in the moment: shame in the stronger man (நாணி), so that sparing is felt as a duty to one's own honour rather than as pity.

gains.a: Nabulan's laughing restraint is given a name as the height of valour, so it is not read as weakness in the middle of a battle
gains.b: the couplet's abstract ஊராண்மை acquires a motive and a gesture, the laugh and the word 'do not fear', that it does not describe

links.note: The Pandya Kudumi warns cows, brahmins, women, the sick and the sonless to take shelter before he shoots; Vipulan will not strike beasts, the wounded, the young or the old.
links.teaches: Both armies spare the weak, but on different grounds: the Purananuru's warning is the way of right (அறத்துஆறு) protecting those who cannot fight, while the epic grounds each refusal in the striker's own glory, so the same restraint can rest on dharma or on pride.

gains.a: Vipulan's code is seen as the epic's version of an old battle rule, and its distinctive turn, honour rather than protection, stands out
gains.b: the Pandya's proclamation gains a contrast that shows how particular its reason is: it names the protected by their vulnerability and their rites, not by what striking them would cost the warrior

links.note: The Kural prefers a spear that missed an elephant to an arrow that hit a hare; Vipulan will not strike even a rutting elephant, since a beast brings no distinction.
links.teaches: The Kural ranks quarry by size and danger and puts the elephant at the top; the epic's warrior ranks by kind and puts every beast below a man, so the two measures of a worthy target diverge exactly at the elephant.

gains.a: the oddity of refusing an elephant in war is sharpened against the proverb that makes the elephant the noblest mark
gains.b: the couplet's scale of targets is shown to be one of several: a code of honour among men can rank the elephant as no target at all

links.note: Nabulan will not strike an unarmed youth or even his elephant; two verses later the narrator states the code of not striking beasts, the wounded or the young.
links.teaches: The scene acts out first and the rule is stated after, so the code of 2261 reads as a summary of how this whole company fights, not as one man's quirk.

links.note: Vipulan offers the enemy heaven in exchange for leaving fame on earth; the challenger who answers him is killed and received into heaven by the celestial women.
links.teaches: The taunt turns out to be a literal promise kept: the one man who takes up Vipulan's offer gets exactly the heaven it named, so the challenge is courtesy as well as threat.

links.note: Purananuru 287 says warriors who do not run, if they die, enjoy the weddings of flawless women in the higher world; in 2265 the slain challenger is showered with flowers by celestial women and reaches heaven.
links.teaches: The Purananuru's reward is promised to one's own unflinching men to steady them; the epic grants it on the field to an enemy killed by the hero's companion, so the heaven of the brave is shown to belong to the fallen of either side.

gains.a: the apsaras' welcome is read as the old Puram reward for the unflinching dead, not a passing ornament
gains.b: the poem's promise, a speech to warriors before battle, is seen fulfilled as an event, and extended to the man who loses a fair duel

links.note: The Kural says one who tends his guests becomes a good guest of those in the sky; Vipulan calls his challenger a guest and gives him the first blow, and it is the guest, killed, who goes to heaven.
links.teaches: Read with the couplet, the duel inverts its exchange: in the Kural the host earns heaven by feeding the guest, while on the battlefield the host's hospitality is the first stroke, and heaven goes to the guest he kills.

gains.a: the word விருந்து in a duel is shown to carry the full weight of the guest-ethic, so the courtesy is not a figure of speech
gains.b: the couplet's tie between hosting and heaven is seen working in a setting it never imagines, where the guest is an enemy and the welcome is death

links.note: The Kampili king dies by arrows in the chest that women's breasts had ploughed; later the warrior whose chest is flushed from pressing women's breasts scatters burning arrows.
links.teaches: The chapter uses the lover's chest twice, once as the place where death enters and once as the source of the killer's fire, so the same mark of love signals both the victim and the victor.

source_issues: 2252 line 1 உழவன மான்றேர் is probably உழவன் மான்றேர் (or உழவன் அமான்றேர்) with a letter misdivided.
2258 line 1 ஏந்தறன் is read as ஏந்தல் தன்.
2260 line 4 (கண்காவல கழுகோம்புவ துயராநனி வினவும்) is hard to construe.
2275 lines 2-4: உடு and வயிரம் are doubtful, and the elephant's part is unclear.
2276 line 4 (பத்திரக் கடிப்பு மின்னப் பகடு போர்த்தான்) is a foot short and repeats the opening of 2277; the end of 2276 may be lost or misplaced.
2252-2259 and 2262-2275 were printed in eight half-lines and joined into four by the tool.
